title: Birth, musical family, uncle teaching him clarinet, first Mardi Gras job
summary: Ford was born in Charity Hospital in 1929; his uncles and cousins were musicians. His uncle started him on clarinet around 1944, he played a Mardi Gras parade with the Eureka band for 15 dollars, then a job with the Adams family group across the river.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: What's my birthday? Here in the Charity Hospital, December 16th, 1929. It's almost happy birthday, five. Yeah, in about another week or so. Six days. Six days. And you were born in Charity
Hospital? Yes. And we were talking about the musicians in your family before we ever had

the machine on. Well, far back as I know, my grandfather was a cornet player, Martin Gabriel. I was a drummer. And his sons, they all played, I believe. Martin Gabriel, I could call him Manny, my Uncle Manny. Uncle Clarence plays piano. Uncle Manny plays saxophone clarinet. He was a drummer with Louis Armstrong before he left New Orleans. And my Uncle August Lundwa, he married mine. He played bass. I know you know him. Uncle Clarence plays bass. And I was there, I have cousins. My Uncle had six boys and they all played. Charles, he and I started out together. He played saxophone, clarinet, flute like I do. He's in Detroit now. Which Uncle? Is this Manny or Clarence? Manny's a person. Now, Uncle Clarence is sons. He doesn't have any musicians in his. He's the only one. And my Uncle Clarence, he didn't have any kids. But my Uncle Manny's the one that's more or less like a second father to the whole family. And my and our brother is like a second mother. Grandfather, I say, you know, she played also. Which I guess you know about that. But my Uncle Manny started me out. I believe I was getting ready. I was about fourteen. I was getting ready to be fifteen. Around this time of year. How it actually started. Charles. Charles was playing already. My little cousin. And I got a picture I can show you all. I'm taking around that time. Charles was blowing the clarinet. I think he was playing Sweet Sue or something like that. It must be 1944. And he said, I bet you can't do this. I said, I bet I could. So I took the horn. It was his father's horn. And I couldn't get a sound out of the horn. It was clarinet. He flat clarinet. And then as I picked up the horn, his father walked in the door. And I said, wow, I'm in for it now. Because see, my Uncle was giving us some whipping if we did something wrong. And he didn't get angry. He said, if you want to learn how to play, I'll show you. And so then Charles, well Charles was one of a fifty-five fifteen children. No, eleven children. And he was a couple of years under me. He was about thirteen at the time. Well, he didn't know me thirteen. I was going to be fifteen. And Charles would have to, being the youngest one, all the older ones worked and left all the dishes to be washed at the house. So when we'd have, I'd help him with his house. We all had housework to do. I'd help him with his housework. And then we'd get the, my Uncle said, we could use the horns after we, after the faster he finished the work, the quicker we could get the horns to practice. So I'd help him with the work. And then we'd practice. Practice over there. About his house. And sometime, uh, his mother said, I don't want all that noise. And we all lived around the corner where, uh, in fact we lived right now around the corner from where my Aunt Albert is living now on the mural. And my Aunt Albert said, I don't want all that noise. So we'd go, we'd come home, my mother said, I don't want all that noise. And then so we finally wound up in a chicken yard, where nothing but chickens would be back there and us. So that's what this picture that I'll show you. And we borrowed my Uncle's caps from the band. We both took it and put them on. And we both had E flat clarinets. And we played, uh, I must have played about six months. And at the time Mardi Gras came around. So it must have been in September, something like that I started. But Mardi Gras came around and he said, uh, get you a job for carnival. And, uh, I didn't know about three tunes because we were learning. We would, we would, we would, we would force that system that my Uncle used. He would learn home sweet home first, which is similar to a scale. And then he'd write out the C scale, then the F scale. And then, uh, well, I, I know it, I knew that, uh, an eighth note got a half a beat and a quarter note got one beat. So, uh, with that I tried to buy some little sheet music and learn tunes, which, the tunes that they were playing in this particular Mardi Gras parade were, like, Who Drew the Whiskey in the Well, Lady Be Good, I believe, When the Saints Go Marching In. Yeah, those three. I can remember. And, uh, my Uncle was supposed to work, but he, people called him, so he said he'd send me, he sent Charles with another, this was the Eureka band that I wanted. I don't believe Sheep was with him at the time. But I remember Kid Shots was in the band, and T-Boy Ray Me was the leader of the band. I remember that. And that was my first professional engagement. That Mardi Gras? That Mardi Gras 19, I believe if there was a Mardi Gras in 45, I'm not sure. Because, see, they cut it out from the wall. I don't know what year. They'd stop Mardi Gras tomorrow? Yeah. I don't know how many years they cut it out. They may have stopped it for two years or three years. But, uh, the first one after, uh, it was the first one after they stopped it. And I don't know if they stopped it in 45, and they started again in 45 rather. Or 45, I believe it was 45. Well, 15. That would have been your first engagement. My first time I meet him. Did you get paid for it? I got 15 dollars. I'll never forget. Wow. Most of mine I never had in my life. That's right. That was a lot, wasn't it? Yeah, but we walked eight hours. Yeah. We walked eight hours. We'd had to walk. And, uh, I was so tired, I couldn't walk and my mouth was so sore. And you kept playing those same three, Terrence? Well, we played those three and the others would be maybe something real easy to catch, something like that. But I remember those three. Something you could improvise really. Yes. And I may have played one or two others, but I don't know. Oh, Panama was another one. Panama too. But when I learned Panama, I didn't learn the whole thing like they do it now. And, uh, just the da-da-da-da-da-da, that's the fault I learned my uncle talking, because it would have been too much trouble to learn that. Mm-hmm. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da, all I'd like I knew it now. But that was E flat climbing. So I said, I started in jazz with Dixonland, and went all the way up to bebop and other things, and then went back to Dixonland. So you've gone. Yeah. I made a cycle. But that was the first job I played for money, period. And the second one was with the Adams family. We kid about that now. With the Placide and Justin? Yeah, their family. They had a family group. The mother played piano. Placide played drums at the time, yeah. Yeah, we played great drums. Uh-huh. And Justin, and Gerald, Gerald played bass. Gerald right now is not active in music. He just gave it up for a while. I guess he would play a game sometime. But Gerald, he's not there, I don't believe he's fifty years old. He's about forty-seven. Because Gerald was a couple of years old. I remember I'm forty-five. Placide and I are the same age. About a few months different. And that was the second job, and I played so bad until they said they wanted somebody to play a little better. Where were you at? Where'd you play? Over the river. In, I believe it was the Moulin Rouge. The Rouge? Yeah. See, at that time, they was working in Algiers and Gretna. There was more work there than it was in the Allers.
